items.readable_text:
Content:
Until now, all limits of the form [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to a} f(x)] that we have encountered have evaluated to either a finite number or [MATH: \text{DNE}.] However, there is another possibility: the limit could be infinite!

Content:
For example, consider the function [MATH: f(x)] whose graph is shown below. This function has a vertical asymptote at [MATH: x=1,] and the function value [MATH: f(x)] grows without bound as [MATH: x] approaches the asymptote [MATH: x=1.] What is the limit [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x)]?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/815fbd2e2e392e274e615b636b76ec3e]

Content:
Remember that in order for computing any limit, in this case, [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x),] we have to compute the left and right-sided limits separately and ensure that they match up.

Content:
- Left-sided limit: As we approach [MATH: x=1] (the vertical asymptote) from the left side of the graph, the function [MATH: f(x)] increases without bound, approaching [MATH: \infty.] We conclude that
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to 1^-} f(x) = \infty.]
- Right-sided limit: Likewise, as we approach the vertical asymptote [MATH: x=1] from the right side of the graph, [MATH: f(x)] still approaches [MATH: \infty.] Consequently,
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to 1^+ } f(x) = \infty.]

Content:
We see that both the left and right limits exist and are equal to [MATH: \infty\mathbin{:}] [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to 1^-} f(x) = \lim_\limits{x\to 1^+} f(x) = \infty]

Content:
As a result, the overall limit is also equal to [MATH: \infty\mathbin{:}] [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x) = \infty]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Until now, all limits of the form [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to a} f(x)] that we have encountered have evaluated to either a finite number or [MATH: \text{DNE}.] However, there is another possibility: the limit could be infinite!

Content:
For example, consider the function [MATH: f(x)] whose graph is shown below. This function has a vertical asymptote at [MATH: x=1,] and the function value [MATH: f(x)] grows without bound as [MATH: x] approaches the asymptote [MATH: x=1.] What is the limit [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x)]?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/815fbd2e2e392e274e615b636b76ec3e]

Content:
Remember that in order for computing any limit, in this case, [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x),] we have to compute the left and right-sided limits separately and ensure that they match up.

Content:
- Left-sided limit: As we approach [MATH: x=1] (the vertical asymptote) from the left side of the graph, the function [MATH: f(x)] increases without bound, approaching [MATH: \infty.] We conclude that
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to 1^-} f(x) = \infty.]
- Right-sided limit: Likewise, as we approach the vertical asymptote [MATH: x=1] from the right side of the graph, [MATH: f(x)] still approaches [MATH: \infty.] Consequently,
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to 1^+ } f(x) = \infty.]

Content:
We see that both the left and right limits exist and are equal to [MATH: \infty\mathbin{:}] [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to 1^-} f(x) = \lim_\limits{x\to 1^+} f(x) = \infty]

Content:
As a result, the overall limit is also equal to [MATH: \infty\mathbin{:}] [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\to 1} f(x) = \infty]

Explanation:
We see from the graph that as [MATH: x] approaches [MATH: 4] from the left, the function [MATH: f(x)] approaches [MATH: -\infty.] So, the left-hand limit is

Consequently,
